ear-training.assumptionNote: Drills play clean sine tones at A4 = 440 Hz reference. Intervals are presented as simple (within one octave); compound intervals like ninths and tenths are not included.
benefits: Build the core musician skill: recognising intervals and chords by ear alone.
Start with 5 easy intervals and grow to all 12 when you are ready.
Instant feedback with score, accuracy, and streak keeps practice honest.
Harmonic mode trains you to hear two notes at once - the real-world listening skill.

faqs.a: An interval is the distance between two notes, measured in semitones. A minor third is 3 semitones (C to Eb), a perfect fifth is 7 (C to G), an octave is 12. Train your ear on the sound of each distance and you can identify any melody's steps.

Learn them in this order: perfect fifth (strong and open), octave (same note, higher), major third (bright), perfect fourth, then minor third. These five are the basic set here. Add minor second and tritone later - they are the hardest to tell apart.
faqs.q: Which intervals should I learn first?

faqs.a: Yes, and they are worth learning: a major triad (C-E-G) sounds bright and resolved, minor (C-Eb-G) sounds darker, diminished (C-Eb-Gb) sounds tense, augmented (C-E-G#) sounds dreamy and unstable. The triad drill plays all four.
faqs.q: What is the difference between major, minor, diminished, and augmented triads?

faqs.a: Melodic means one note after the other (easier - you compare two clear pitches). Harmonic means both notes at the same time (harder - you must pick the blend apart). Master melodic first, then switch on harmonic mode for the real challenge.
faqs.q: Melodic or harmonic intervals - which is harder?

faqs.a: Ten focused minutes daily beats an hour once a week. Aim for 80% accuracy on the basic set before moving to the full 12 intervals. Your brain builds pitch memory during sleep, so short daily sessions compound fast.
faqs.q: How long should I practise each day?

faqs.a: Relative pitch is learnable by almost everyone; perfect pitch (naming any note cold) is rare and mostly set in childhood. This tool trains relative pitch - hearing distances between notes - which is the skill working musicians actually use.

ear-training.formula:
Interval size in semitones:
m2=1, M2=2, m3=3, M3=4, P4=5, tritone=6,
P5=7, m6=8, M6=9, m7=10, M7=11, octave=12.
Triads: major = 0-4-7, minor = 0-3-7,
diminished = 0-3-6, augmented = 0-4-8.
howTo: Choose your drill: intervals or triads.
For intervals, pick the basic set (5 easy intervals) or the full set (all 12).
Tap New round to hear the mystery sound. Replay it as often as you like.
Click the answer you hear. The correct button turns green; a wrong pick turns red.
Watch your score and streak - the next round starts automatically.
keyFacts: An interval is the distance between two notes: a perfect fifth is 7 semitones, an octave is 12.
The basic set (major 2nd, major 3rd, perfect 4th, perfect 5th, octave) covers most melodies.
A major triad is 0-4-7 semitones; minor is 0-3-7; diminished 0-3-6; augmented 0-4-8.
Melodic intervals play notes one after another; harmonic intervals play them together.
Ten focused minutes a day builds pitch memory faster than one long weekly session.
Relative pitch (hearing distances) is learnable by almost everyone with practice.
ear-training.keywords: ear training, interval ear training, chord ear training, music ear training online, interval recognition
limitations: Sine tones only - real instruments have richer harmonics that change how intervals sound.
Simple intervals only; compound intervals (9ths, 11ths) are not included.
Random base notes stay within one octave of middle C, not the full instrument range.
No rhythm or melody context - isolated drills are the starting point, not the whole skill.

ear-training.workedExample:
Interval drill, basic set:
1. Tap New round. You hear two notes: C4 then G4 (a perfect fifth, 7 semitones).
2. You click Perfect 5th. Green - correct. Score 1/1, streak 1.
3. Next: C4 then F4 (perfect fourth, 5 semitones). You click Perfect 4th. Correct again.
4. Next: C4 then E4 (major third). You click Minor 3rd - red. The right answer (Major 3rd) turns green.
5. After 20 rounds at 16/20, your accuracy is 80% - time to try the full set.
